tips.title: Rate is amount over time
tips.body:
$$\text{mean rate} = \frac{\text{quantity used or made}}{\text{time taken}}$$

It does not matter whether you measure a **reactant used up** or a **product formed** — both give the rate. The unit comes from the division: cm³ per second is **cm³/s**, grams per second is **g/s**.

tips.title: Mean rate and rate at a moment are different
tips.body: Dividing the **total** amount by the **total** time gives the **mean** rate over the whole reaction. The rate at **one instant** is the **gradient of a tangent** at that point. A question naming a specific time wants the tangent, not the mean.

tips.title: The curve flattens because reactants run out
tips.body: Every rate graph is **steepest at the start** and **levels off** at the end. Steepest at the start because the reactants are at their **most concentrated**; level at the end because a reactant has been **used up**, so no more product forms.

tips.title: Five factors
tips.body: **Concentration** of reactants in solution, **pressure** of reacting gases, **surface area** of solid reactants, **temperature**, and the presence of a **catalyst**. Pressure applies to **gases** only and concentration to **solutions** only, so a question about a solid and an acid is not asking about pressure.

tips.title: Powder means more surface area
tips.body: Breaking a solid into smaller pieces does not change its mass, but it **exposes more surface**. A 3 : 1 surface area to volume ratio becomes 6 : 1 when the cube's side is halved — so more particles are available to collide, and the reaction is faster.

why.matters:
Knowing that a reaction happens is not much use on its own. A process that takes a fortnight is not worth running, and one that finishes in a tenth of a second is an explosion — so the question industry and the laboratory actually ask is **how fast**, and what changes it.

Measuring it turns out to be simple: follow one thing that changes — a gas collected, a mass falling, a cross disappearing — and watch the clock. The graph that comes out tells the whole story of the reaction.

examples.title: Why the fizzing always slows down
examples.body:
Drop a tablet in water and the first few seconds are furious, then it calms, then it stops. Every rate graph anyone plots has that shape, and both ends of it mean something.

It is steepest at the **start** because that is when the reactants are most concentrated, so collisions are most frequent. It flattens because a reactant is running out. And when the line goes horizontal the reaction has **finished** — not slowed down, finished, because there is nothing left to react.

visual.alt: A curve of gas given off against time that rises steeply at first and then gradually flattens to a horizontal line, the shape every rate graph takes as the reactants are used up

examples.title: Two ways to watch the same reaction
examples.body:
You cannot measure a reaction directly. You pick something it changes and follow **that**, and the choice depends on what the reaction gives you.

If it makes a gas, collect it in a syringe and read the volume, or stand the flask on a balance and watch the mass fall as the gas escapes. If it makes a cloudy precipitate instead, put a paper cross under the flask and time how long it takes to disappear. Different quantity, same rate — and the second needs nothing but a stopwatch.

visual.alt: A table of three ways to follow a reaction: the volume of gas in a syringe giving a rate in cubic centimetres per second, the mass lost on a balance giving grams per second, and the time for a cross to disappear

examples.title: The mean rate and the rate right now
examples.body:
A reaction gives off 60 cm³ of gas in 25 seconds, so its mean rate is **2.4 cm³/s**. That is a real number and it describes no moment of the reaction at all.

At the start this one was running at **twice** that — the steepest part of the curve — and at the end it was doing nothing. The mean is the straight line from beginning to end; the rate at a moment is the **gradient of a tangent**. A question that names a time is asking for the tangent, and the two answers are different on purpose.

visual.alt: A curve of gas against time reaching sixty cubic centimetres at twenty-five seconds, with two straight lines from the origin: the steeper one the rate at the start and the shallower one the mean rate over the whole reaction

steps.title: Calculating a mean rate
steps.body:
**The rate of a chemical reaction can be found by measuring the quantity of a reactant used or the quantity of product formed over time.**

$$\text{mean rate of reaction} = \frac{\text{quantity of reactant used}}{\text{time taken}}$$

$$\text{mean rate of reaction} = \frac{\text{quantity of product formed}}{\text{time taken}}$$

**The quantity can be a mass in grams or a volume in cm³**, so the units of rate are **g/s** or **cm³/s**. At Higher tier, quantities may be in **moles**, giving **mol/s**.

**Either measurement works**, because a reactant disappearing and a product appearing are the same event seen from two sides.

steps.title: Reading a rate graph
steps.body:
**Plotting quantity of product against time gives a curve with a characteristic shape**: steep at first, then gradually flattening until it is horizontal.

**Why it starts steepest.** At the beginning the reactants are at their **highest concentration**, so collisions are most frequent and the reaction is fastest.

**Why it flattens.** As the reaction proceeds the reactants are **used up**, so collisions become less frequent and the reaction slows.

**Why it becomes horizontal.** The reaction has **finished** — one of the reactants has been **completely used up**, so no more product can form. The height of the flat section is the **total amount of product**.

**Two different quantities can be read off the same curve**, and questions distinguish them carefully:

- The **mean rate** over a period is the **total quantity divided by the total time** — in effect the gradient of a straight line between the two points.
- The **rate at a particular moment** is the **gradient of the tangent** drawn to the curve at that point.

**Comparing two curves.** A **steeper** curve means a **faster** reaction. If two curves finish at the **same height**, the **same amount of product** was made and only the **rate** differed — which is exactly what changing temperature, concentration, surface area or adding a catalyst does. If one finishes **higher**, there was **more reactant**.

steps.title: Rate at a moment: the tangent
steps.body:
**The rate at a particular time is the gradient of the curve at that time**, and you find it by **drawing a tangent** — a straight line just touching the curve at that point — and calculating its gradient.

$$\text{gradient} = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}$$

**At Higher tier you are asked to calculate that gradient**; at Foundation you use the slope of the tangent as a **measure** of rate, comparing steepness rather than working out a number.

**Draw the tangent long.** A short tangent gives a small rise and run, and small measurements carry large percentage errors. Extending it across a good part of the graph makes the calculation far more reliable.

steps.title: The five factors
steps.body:
**Factors which affect the rates of chemical reactions include:**

- the **concentration of reactants in solution**
- the **pressure of reacting gases**
- the **surface area of solid reactants**
- the **temperature**
- the presence of **catalysts**

**Each applies to a particular kind of reactant**, and questions are set on noticing which:

- **Concentration** applies to substances **in solution**.
- **Pressure** applies to **gases** only. A reaction between a solid and an acid is not affected by pressure.
- **Surface area** applies to **solid** reactants. Powder reacts faster than lumps.

**Why surface area works.** Breaking a solid into smaller pieces does not change how much there is — it changes how much of it is **exposed**. A cube of side 2 has a surface area to volume ratio of **3 : 1**; halve the side and the ratio becomes **6 : 1**. More exposed surface means more particles available to be collided with, so the reaction goes faster.

**Temperature and catalysts** are dealt with fully in the next topic, because both need collision theory to explain.

**A caution about catalysts.** A catalyst **changes the rate** but is **not used up**. So it does not appear in the chemical equation, and at the end of the reaction it is still there.

steps.title: Core practical: how concentration affects rate
steps.body:
**This is required practical 5**, and the spec asks for **two** methods: one measuring the **volume of a gas produced**, and one measuring a **change in colour or turbidity**.

**Method 1: measuring gas volume.** Magnesium ribbon and dilute hydrochloric acid, with the hydrogen collected in a **gas syringe**.

1. Measure a set volume of acid of known concentration into a conical flask.
2. Add a measured length of magnesium ribbon and **immediately** stopper the flask and start the stopwatch.
3. Record the **volume of gas** every **10 seconds**.
4. Repeat with different **concentrations** of acid, keeping everything else the same.

Plot volume against time. The **steeper** the curve, the faster the reaction.

**Method 2: the disappearing cross.** Sodium thiosulfate solution and dilute hydrochloric acid, which produce a **precipitate of sulfur** that makes the mixture **cloudy**.

1. Draw a **cross** on paper and stand the flask on it.
2. Mix the two solutions and start the stopwatch.
3. Record the **time for the cross to disappear** when viewed from above.
4. Repeat at different concentrations of thiosulfate.

**Here the rate is $\dfrac{1}{\text{time}}$**, because a **shorter** time means a **faster** reaction.

**Why two methods.** They measure different things — one follows a **product appearing**, the other follows **cloudiness developing** — and each suits a different reaction. The cross method needs no gas-tight apparatus; the syringe method gives a **continuous** record rather than a single endpoint.

**Control variables** matter in both: **temperature** especially, and the **volumes** used, the **amount** of the other reactant, and for the cross method the **same observer** and the **same cross**, since judging when it disappears is subjective.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Mean rate and instantaneous rate are different quantities.** Dividing the **total** by the **total** gives the **mean** over the whole reaction. The rate **at a moment** is the **gradient of a tangent** at that point. Because the reaction slows as it goes, the rate at the start is always **greater** than the mean, and the rate at the end always **smaller**. A question naming a time wants the **tangent**.

**Draw the tangent long.** Rise and run measured over a short stretch carry large percentage errors, and the gradient is a ratio of the two. Extending the tangent across a good part of the graph is the single most useful piece of technique here.

**Height and steepness answer different questions.** **Steepness** is about **rate**; the **final height** is about **amount**. So two curves that level off at the **same height** used the **same quantity of reactant** and differed only in **rate** — which is what a change in concentration, temperature, surface area or a catalyst does. A curve levelling off **higher** means **more reactant was used**, which is a different experiment.

**Surface area changes exposure, not amount.** Powdering a solid leaves the **mass unchanged**, so the **same total product** is made; what changes is **how much surface is available to collide with**. That is why the powdered run is **steeper** but finishes at the **same height** — a pairing questions test repeatedly.

**Match the factor to the state of the reactant.** **Pressure** is for **gases**; **concentration** is for **solutions**; **surface area** is for **solids**. Offering pressure for a reaction between marble chips and acid shows the list has been memorised without being understood.

**Times and rates run in opposite directions.** In the disappearing cross method the measurement is a **time**, and a **shorter** time means a **faster** reaction. Converting to $\dfrac{1}{\text{time}}$ before plotting makes a higher number mean faster, and it gives a free check: **halving the time must double the rate**.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would investigate the effect of acid concentration on the rate of reaction between magnesium and hydrochloric acid, and explain how you would use the results to compare rates.
questions.solution:
I would measure a fixed volume of dilute hydrochloric acid of known concentration into a **conical flask**, then add a measured length of **magnesium ribbon**, **immediately** stopper the flask and start a **stopwatch**. The hydrogen produced is collected in a **gas syringe**, and I would record the **volume of gas every 10 seconds** until the reaction stopped.

Stoppering the flask quickly matters: any gas that escapes before the bung is in is not measured, and because the reaction is **fastest at the start** that is exactly when the most gas is being produced.

I would then repeat the experiment with acid of **different concentrations** — the **independent variable** — keeping everything else the same. The **control variables** include the **temperature**, the **volume of acid**, the **length and mass of magnesium ribbon**, and the **size of the flask**. Temperature matters most, because it is another of the five factors affecting rate: if it varied, I could not tell whether a change in rate was caused by the concentration or by the warmth.

Plotting **volume of gas against time** for each concentration gives a family of curves. Each is **steepest at the start**, because the reactants are then at their **highest concentration**, and each **flattens** and finally becomes **horizontal** when a reactant has been **completely used up**.

Comparing them, the **steeper** the curve, the **faster** the reaction — so the more concentrated the acid, the steeper the curve. For a numerical comparison I could calculate the **mean rate** as the **total volume divided by the total time**, or find the rate at a particular moment by **drawing a tangent** to the curve at that point and calculating its **gradient**, rise over run. The tangent should be drawn **long**, because a short rise and run carry large percentage errors.

One further point worth noting: if the **same mass of magnesium** is used each time, every curve should level off at the **same height**, because the same amount of hydrogen is ultimately produced. Only the **steepness** changes. A run that finished at a different height would suggest a different amount of magnesium had been used, not a different rate.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between the mean rate of a reaction and the rate at a particular moment, how each is found from a graph, and why the two differ.
questions.solution:
The **mean rate** is the rate averaged over a whole period. It is found by dividing the **total quantity** of reactant used or product formed by the **total time taken**:

$$\text{mean rate} = \frac{\text{quantity}}{\text{time}}$$

On a graph this is effectively the gradient of a **straight line drawn between the two end points** of the period.

The **rate at a particular moment** is a different quantity. Because a rate curve is **curved**, its steepness is changing continuously, and the rate at one instant is the **gradient of the curve at that point**. To find it you **draw a tangent** — a straight line just touching the curve at that point — and calculate its gradient as **rise ÷ run**. At Higher tier this calculation is required; otherwise the slope of the tangent is used as a **measure** of rate, for comparison rather than as a number.

The two differ because the **rate is not constant**. At the start the reactants are at their **highest concentration**, so collisions are most frequent and the reaction is at its **fastest** — the curve is **steepest**. As the reaction proceeds the reactants are **used up**, collisions become less frequent, and the reaction **slows**. Eventually one reactant is **completely consumed**, the curve becomes **horizontal**, and the rate is **zero**.

It follows that the **mean rate must lie between** the initial rate and the final rate. The rate at the start is always **greater** than the mean, and the rate near the end always **smaller**. So a question asking for the rate **at 20 seconds** is not answered by dividing the total by the total — that gives the mean, which will generally be wrong for any specific moment.

One practical point makes a real difference to the accuracy of a tangent calculation: **draw the tangent long**. The gradient is a **ratio of two measured lengths**, so an error in each propagates into the answer. Measuring a small rise over a small run means a small absolute error is a **large percentage** of the value, whereas extending the tangent across a substantial part of the graph makes both measurements large and the ratio far more reliable.

examTechnique.body:
Two calculations and one graph. The calculations are **mean rate = quantity ÷ time** and **gradient = rise ÷ run**, and the question tells you which by whether it names a **specific time**.

On the graph, keep **steepness** and **final height** apart: steepness is **rate**, height is **amount**. Most of the harder questions in this topic are that distinction in some form.
examinerErrors: Giving the **mean rate** when the question asks for the rate **at a particular time**.
Drawing a **short tangent**, so the gradient carries a large percentage error.
Saying a faster reaction produces **more product**, when it produces the same amount **sooner**.
Saying powdered solid gives **more gas** than lumps of the same mass.
Offering **pressure** as a factor for a reaction between a solid and a solution.
Plotting **raw times** in the disappearing cross experiment instead of **1 ÷ time**.
Omitting the **unit** from a rate, or giving g/s when a volume was measured.
Forgetting to control **temperature** when investigating concentration.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer reads a rate graph on two axes of meaning at once: **steepness is rate, height is amount**, so it can say that a powdered sample reacts **faster but produces the same volume of gas**, and explain why. It knows the **mean** must lie between the **initial** and **final** rates, and reaches for a **tangent** whenever a moment is named — drawn **long**, with the reason. It matches each factor to the **state** of the reactant, so it rules pressure out for a solid and a solution. And in the cross method it converts **time to 1 ÷ time** before comparing, because rate and time run in opposite directions.
